passage:
Maria: Papa, can I ask about the Saturday job at the bakery near school? 🙂
Arnab: Tell me the details first.
Maria: Ten to two, packing boxes and helping at the counter. Not the ovens. Mrs Pinto said she'll pay weekly.
Arnab: Daytime, inside a shop we know. Good. What about school hours?
Maria: Saturdays only. Homework Sunday morning as usual.
Arnab: I'll ask the school office what the rules are for your age before you say yes. Don't accept anything yet.
Maria: Okay. Should I come along when you visit her?
Arnab: Yes, and Mummy too. We'll all look at the timings together.
Maria: Thank you for not saying no straight away 👍
Arnab: I'm glad you asked me first.

qa.q: What will Maria do at the bakery?
qa.a: Pack boxes and help at the counter, not work at the ovens.

qa.q: What might Maria be feeling when thanking Arnab for not saying no straight away?
qa.a: Relief and a bit of hope: Maria expected a quick refusal and is glad Papa is listening.

qa.q: What else could Maria do to keep the plan safe, and why?
qa.a: Maria could bring the bakery owner's written timings and duties to the family visit, because clear written details make it easier for everyone to check the work suits Maria's age.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Arnab?
qa.a: Arnab is glad to be asked first, and checking the place, daylight hours and the school's rules lets him say yes with confidence rather than worry.

grounding: A student discusses the job with parents, confirms it is age-appropriate, in daylight and safe, and checks the rules first.

subtype: Approach: checking legal and safety limits with parents [Action]
passage:
In the small town of Sehore, Imran had been offered work at the new mobile shop in the bazaar: repairing phones after school. He was sixteen. The owner said, "Come any time, stay till ten."

That evening he sat with his parents on the terrace. His mother, Sangeeta, asked the questions he hadn't. "Till ten at night? Who else works there? Is it on the main road or in the back lane?"

His father added, "And the rules? You're a minor."

The next day Imran asked his teacher, who showed him a government page about work allowed for teenagers: no night shifts, no hazardous work, not during school hours.

So they went together to the shop owner. His father said, "Four to seven, Saturdays and two weekdays, in the front counter area only." The owner agreed.

On the walk home, Imran said, "I thought you'd just say no." His mother smiled. "We just wanted it safe."

qa.q: What hours did Imran's father agree with the shop owner?
qa.a: Four to seven, Saturdays and two weekdays, in the front counter area only.

qa.q: How did Imran feel on the walk home?
qa.a: Imran felt relieved and surprised, having expected his parents to simply refuse.

qa.q: What else could Imran check once he starts working?
qa.a: He could tell his parents at once if the owner asks him to stay late or do risky tasks, so the agreed limits hold.

qa.q: How did the plan look to Sangeeta?
qa.a: Sangeeta wanted to support Imran while keeping him safe, so she asked about the hours, the people and the location before agreeing.

grounding: Shows a student discussing a job with parents, checking the rules on work allowed for teenagers, and making sure the work is in daylight, safe and age-appropriate.

subtype: Approach: checking legal and safety limits with parents [Action]
passage:
In Marseille, Fatima found a notice in the bakery window: "Weekend help wanted, early mornings." She was fifteen. The bakery was a ten-minute walk from home.

At dinner she told her parents. Her father, Sami, didn't say no. He said, "Let's look at the rules together first."

After dinner they sat at the laptop and read the official government page about work for under-sixteens. There were limits: only light work, only during school holidays, a maximum number of hours, and a parent's written consent.

"Early mornings," her mother said. "How early?"

Fatima called the baker the next day. Five a.m. for the kneading shift. That was not allowed at her age.

"But I can do Saturday afternoons at the counter, in the holidays," Fatima reported. "From two to six."

Sami signed the consent form. "Daylight, near home, and legal. Good."

qa.q: What hours could Fatima work at the counter?
qa.a: Saturday afternoons in the holidays, from two to six.

qa.q: How might Fatima have felt when she learned the five a.m. shift was not allowed?
qa.a: She may have felt a little disappointed, but also satisfied to find a safe, legal option instead.

qa.q: What else should Fatima and her parents keep an eye on?
qa.a: They should make sure the counter job stays light and within the hours agreed, and speak up if the baker asks for more.

qa.q: How does Sami see the final arrangement?
qa.a: Sami seems satisfied and reassured, signing the form because the work is in daylight, near home and legal.

grounding: Shows a teen checking a job's legal limits with parents and choosing daylight hours in a safe place near home before accepting.
